taxonomy.subtopic: Usual interstitial pneumonia, fibroblastic foci, and basal subpleural honeycombing

questions.stem_html: A 68-year-old man has 18 months of progressive exertional dyspnea and a nonproductive cough. Examination shows digital clubbing and fine inspiratory crackles at both lung bases. The accompanying high-resolution chest diagram shows peripheral, basal reticulation with traction bronchiectasis and stacked subpleural cysts. A biopsy schematic shows alternating normal lung, dense collagen, and fibroblastic foci. Which mediator most directly promotes the fibroblast activation and extracellular-matrix deposition underlying this disorder?

options.text_html: Interferon-gamma
Transforming growth factor-beta
Interleukin-5
Bradykinin
Vascular endothelial growth factor

questions.explanation_html: The clinical, radiographic, and histologic pattern is usual interstitial pneumonia, the characteristic pattern of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. Repetitive alveolar epithelial injury leads to an abnormal repair response in which transforming growth factor-beta promotes fibroblast differentiation, myofibroblast activity, and collagen-rich extracellular-matrix deposition. Temporal heterogeneity and fibroblastic foci distinguish UIP from more uniform inflammatory interstitial patterns.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Interferon-gamma favors macrophage activation and cell-mediated immunity and is not the principal profibrotic driver in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Interleukin-5 promotes eosinophil differentiation and survival, as in eosinophilic and allergic disorders.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Bradykinin increases vascular permeability and contributes to cough and angioedema but does not explain progressive subpleural fibrosis.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Vascular endothelial growth factor promotes angiogenesis and vascular permeability rather than the core fibroblast program shown.

questions.educational_objective: Usual interstitial pneumonia combines basal subpleural honeycombing and temporally heterogeneous fibroblastic foci; TGF-beta is a central profibrotic mediator.

media.alt_text: Original paired schematic showing basal subpleural honeycombing on chest imaging and patchy fibroblastic foci beside dense fibrosis on histology.

references.citation: USMLE. Step 1 Exam Content: Content Outline and Specifications. Accessed August 4, 2026.
Raghu G et al. Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (an Update) and Progressive Pulmonary Fibrosis in Adults. Am J Respir Crit Care Med. 2022;205:e18-e47.

taxonomy.subtopic: GLUT1-positive proliferative and involution phases

questions.stem_html: A healthy infant has no visible lesion at birth. At 3 weeks of age, a small red papule appears on the cheek and enlarges rapidly over the next 4 months into a bright-red, compressible plaque. The accompanying timeline shows rapid early growth followed by gradual replacement with fibrofatty tissue. Biopsy demonstrates tightly packed capillary channels whose endothelial cells stain for GLUT1. Which diagnosis best fits these findings?

options.text_html: Capillary malformation
Venous malformation
Infantile hemangioma
Pyogenic granuloma
Rapidly involuting congenital hemangioma

questions.explanation_html: Infantile hemangioma is a benign endothelial tumor that typically becomes apparent during the first weeks after birth, undergoes a proliferative phase, and later involutes. GLUT1 positivity is a characteristic diagnostic feature. Vascular malformations are structural anomalies that are generally present at birth and grow proportionally with the child rather than following a proliferative-involutional life cycle.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Capillary malformations are usually present at birth and persist rather than undergoing rapid postnatal proliferation followed by involution.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: Venous malformations are congenital structural lesions with slow-flow venous channels and do not show the classic GLUT1-positive life cycle.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Pyogenic granuloma is a rapidly growing lobular capillary proliferation often triggered by trauma or pregnancy and does not follow the infantile hemangioma timeline.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Rapidly involuting congenital hemangioma is fully formed at birth and is generally GLUT1-negative.

questions.educational_objective: Infantile hemangiomas are GLUT1-positive endothelial tumors that appear after birth, proliferate rapidly in infancy, and then involute.

media.alt_text: Original timeline and capillary-channel schematic showing postnatal proliferation, plateau, involution, and GLUT1-positive endothelium.

references.citation: USMLE. Step 1 Exam Content: Content Outline and Specifications. Accessed August 4, 2026.
Krowchuk DP et al. Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Infantile Hemangiomas. Pediatrics. 2019;143:e20183475.

taxonomy.subtopic: HPV16 E6/E7, p53/RB disruption, and p16 overexpression

questions.stem_html: A 47-year-old man who has never smoked presents with a painless cervical lymph node and a small tonsillar mass. Biopsy shows nonkeratinizing squamous-cell carcinoma with strong, diffuse p16 immunostaining. The accompanying molecular diagram shows two viral oncoproteins acting on cell-cycle checkpoints. Which event most directly explains the p16 overexpression in this tumor?

options.text_html: E6-mediated stabilization of p53
E6-mediated activation of RB
E7-mediated degradation of p16
E7-mediated inactivation of RB with release of E2F
Integration-driven activation of BCL2

questions.explanation_html: High-risk HPV-associated oropharyngeal carcinoma commonly shows strong p16 expression. Viral E7 binds and functionally inactivates the RB tumor suppressor, releasing E2F and driving cell-cycle entry. Loss of RB-mediated negative feedback produces compensatory p16 overexpression, making p16 a useful surrogate marker for transcriptionally active HPV in the appropriate oropharyngeal context. E6 instead promotes p53 degradation.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: E6 promotes p53 degradation rather than stabilization and does not directly create the characteristic p16 feedback pattern.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: E6 targets p53-associated pathways, not RB activation.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: E7 does not cause p16 degradation; p16 rises because RB signaling is disabled.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: BCL2 activation is not the defining molecular explanation for diffuse p16 expression in HPV-associated oropharyngeal carcinoma.

questions.educational_objective: HPV E7 inactivates RB, releases E2F, and produces compensatory p16 overexpression; E6 promotes p53 degradation.

media.alt_text: Original tonsillar and molecular schematic linking HPV E6 to p53 loss and E7 to RB inactivation, E2F release, and p16 overexpression.

references.citation: USMLE. Step 1 Exam Content: Content Outline and Specifications. Accessed August 4, 2026.
National Cancer Institute. HPV and Cancer; Oropharyngeal Cancer. Accessed August 4, 2026.

taxonomy.subtopic: Bladder outlet obstruction, bilateral hydronephrosis, and oligohydramnios

questions.stem_html: Prenatal ultrasonography of a male fetus shows a markedly distended thick-walled bladder, dilation of the proximal urethra, and bilateral hydroureteronephrosis. Amniotic fluid volume is severely reduced. After delivery, the newborn has immediate respiratory distress. Which process most directly caused the respiratory abnormality?

options.text_html: Surfactant inactivation by aspirated meconium
Pulmonary edema from left-to-right ductal shunting
Congenital absence of type II pneumocytes
Airway compression by an enlarged bladder
Pulmonary hypoplasia caused by prolonged oligohydramnios

questions.explanation_html: Posterior urethral valves produce fetal bladder-outlet obstruction in males. Severe obstruction reduces fetal urine output, causing oligohydramnios. Adequate amniotic fluid is required for normal lung expansion and development; prolonged oligohydramnios therefore causes pulmonary hypoplasia and severe neonatal respiratory distress. The urinary tract findings, including a dilated posterior urethra and distended bladder, support this diagnosis.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Meconium aspiration causes chemical pneumonitis and air trapping but does not explain the prenatal urinary tract abnormalities and oligohydramnios.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: Ductal shunting can cause pulmonary overcirculation after birth, not the reduced lung growth associated with low amniotic fluid.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Type II pneumocytes are present in pulmonary hypoplasia; the problem is inadequate lung growth rather than selective absence of one cell type.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Bladder enlargement does not directly compress the thorax enough to produce this characteristic respiratory syndrome.

questions.educational_objective: Severe posterior urethral obstruction lowers fetal urine production, causing oligohydramnios and secondary pulmonary hypoplasia.

media.alt_text: Original fetal urinary-tract schematic showing the keyhole sign, distended bladder, bilateral hydronephrosis, oligohydramnios, and small lungs.

references.citation: USMLE. Step 1 Exam Content: Content Outline and Specifications. Accessed August 4, 2026.
NCBI Bookshelf. Posterior Urethral Valves. Updated 2024. Accessed August 4, 2026.

taxonomy.subtopic: Hapten-specific type IV delayed hypersensitivity

questions.stem_html: A woman develops intensely pruritic, vesicular erythema beneath a nickel-containing watchband 48 hours after wearing it. She had a milder reaction at the same site several months earlier. The accompanying diagram separates an initial sensitization phase from a later elicitation phase. Which mechanism best explains the recurrent eruption?

options.text_html: A small chemical binds epidermal proteins, is presented by cutaneous dendritic cells, and elicits memory T-cell inflammation on re-exposure
Preformed IgE on mast cells cross-links within minutes of antigen contact
Circulating IgG binds a fixed basement-membrane antigen and activates complement
Soluble antigen-antibody complexes deposit in dermal venules
A microbial superantigen cross-links MHC class II and T-cell receptors

questions.explanation_html: Nickel acts as a hapten: it binds host proteins, creating neoantigens that are processed by epidermal dendritic cells and presented during sensitization. On re-exposure, hapten-specific memory T cells produce a delayed type IV reaction with cytokine release, keratinocyte injury, spongiosis, and vesiculation. The 24- to 72-hour timing distinguishes this from immediate IgE-mediated hypersensitivity.

wrong_choice_explanations.2: IgE-mediated mast-cell activation produces an immediate type I reaction, often within minutes, rather than a delayed eczematous eruption.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Antibody binding to fixed tissue antigens describes type II hypersensitivity, such as autoimmune blistering disease.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Immune-complex deposition describes type III hypersensitivity and is not the mechanism of localized nickel dermatitis.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Superantigen activation causes broad, non-antigen-specific T-cell stimulation rather than hapten-specific contact dermatitis.

questions.educational_objective: Allergic contact dermatitis is a type IV reaction in which haptens modify skin proteins, dendritic cells prime T cells, and memory T cells drive delayed inflammation on re-exposure.

media.alt_text: Original two-phase diagram showing hapten-protein formation, dendritic-cell migration, T-cell sensitization, and delayed skin inflammation after re-exposure.

references.citation: USMLE. Step 1 Exam Content: Content Outline and Specifications. Accessed August 4, 2026.
NCBI Bookshelf. Type IV Hypersensitivity Reaction. Updated 2025. Accessed August 4, 2026.

taxonomy.subtopic: Breslow depth and vertical growth as prognostic determinants

questions.stem_html: An asymmetric pigmented lesion is excised from a patient's upper back. Histology shows malignant melanocytes spreading laterally within the epidermis and invading vertically into the dermis. The accompanying skin diagram marks a depth of 2.6 mm from the granular layer to the deepest malignant cell. In a melanoma clinically confined to the primary site, which feature most strongly predicts the risk of nodal or distant spread?

options.text_html: Total surface diameter of the lesion
Vertical tumor thickness measured in millimeters
Amount of melanin pigment in tumor cells
Presence of a surrounding lymphocytic infiltrate
Anatomic location on the trunk rather than an extremity

questions.explanation_html: Breslow thickness measures the vertical depth of melanoma from the top of the granular layer, or from the base of an ulcer, to the deepest malignant cell. Increasing thickness is strongly associated with regional and distant metastasis and is central to staging and management. Radial growth describes lateral spread; acquisition of vertical growth permits deeper invasion and metastatic access.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Diameter is clinically useful when identifying suspicious lesions but is less predictive than histologic depth after melanoma is diagnosed.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Melanin content varies widely and does not provide the principal prognostic measurement.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Host lymphocytic response can have prognostic associations but is not the primary staging variable illustrated.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Anatomic site affects management context but does not replace Breslow thickness as the key local prognostic measure.

questions.educational_objective: Breslow thickness quantifies vertical invasion and is a major prognostic determinant for localized cutaneous melanoma.

media.alt_text: Original skin cross-section showing radial epidermal spread, vertical dermal invasion, and a Breslow depth measurement line.

references.citation: USMLE. Step 1 Exam Content: Content Outline and Specifications. Accessed August 4, 2026.
National Cancer Institute. Melanoma Treatment (PDQ): Stage Information. Updated 2025. Accessed August 4, 2026.

taxonomy.subtopic: Fanconi syndrome and generalized proximal solute wasting

questions.stem_html: A man receiving long-term tenofovir develops fatigue and bone pain. Serum glucose is normal, but urinalysis shows glucose, phosphate, amino acids, and low-molecular-weight proteins. Laboratory studies show hypophosphatemia and a hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis. The accompanying nephron map highlights one tubular segment. Dysfunction of which segment best explains the complete pattern?

options.text_html: Thin descending limb
Thick ascending limb
Proximal convoluted tubule
Distal convoluted tubule
Cortical collecting duct

questions.explanation_html: Fanconi syndrome is generalized proximal tubular dysfunction. The proximal convoluted tubule normally reabsorbs filtered glucose, amino acids, phosphate, bicarbonate, uric acid, and low-molecular-weight proteins. Injury therefore causes normoglycemic glucosuria, aminoaciduria, phosphaturia, and bicarbonate loss, producing type 2 renal tubular acidosis and phosphate-depletion bone disease.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: The thin descending limb primarily permits water reabsorption and does not reclaim the broad group of solutes lost here.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: The thick ascending limb reabsorbs sodium, potassium, and chloride through NKCC2; its dysfunction resembles Bartter syndrome and causes alkalosis.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: The distal convoluted tubule reabsorbs sodium chloride and calcium but does not account for glucosuria and aminoaciduria.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Collecting-duct defects alter acid, potassium, or water handling rather than causing generalized filtered-solute wasting.

questions.educational_objective: Fanconi syndrome localizes to the proximal tubule and causes urinary loss of glucose, phosphate, amino acids, bicarbonate, and low-molecular-weight proteins.

media.alt_text: Original nephron diagram highlighting proximal-tubule reabsorption of glucose, phosphate, amino acids, and bicarbonate with urinary loss in Fanconi syndrome.

references.citation: USMLE. Step 1 Exam Content: Content Outline and Specifications. Accessed August 4, 2026.
NCBI Bookshelf. Fanconi Syndrome. Updated June 24, 2025. Accessed August 4, 2026.

taxonomy.subtopic: Malignant osteoid, metaphyseal growth, and RB1 association

questions.stem_html: A 15-year-old boy has progressive pain and swelling above the knee. An original radiographic schematic shows a destructive metaphyseal lesion of the distal femur with a sunburst periosteal reaction and elevation of the periosteum. Biopsy demonstrates pleomorphic malignant cells directly producing lace-like osteoid. Germline loss of which tumor-suppressor gene most strongly predisposes to this tumor?

options.text_html: APC
VHL
NF2
RB1
MEN1

questions.explanation_html: The lesion is osteosarcoma, defined histologically by malignant cells producing osteoid. It commonly arises in the metaphysis of long bones near the knee and may produce a sunburst pattern or Codman triangle. Germline RB1 mutations predispose to retinoblastoma and later osteosarcoma; TP53 defects such as Li-Fraumeni syndrome are another important association.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: APC loss predisposes to familial adenomatous polyposis and colorectal neoplasia, not the classic osteosarcoma-retinoblastoma pairing.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: VHL loss predisposes to clear-cell renal carcinoma, hemangioblastomas, and pheochromocytoma.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: NF2 loss predisposes to bilateral vestibular schwannomas and meningiomas.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: MEN1 loss predisposes to parathyroid, pancreatic neuroendocrine, and pituitary tumors.

questions.educational_objective: Osteosarcoma is a metaphyseal malignant bone tumor that produces osteoid and is associated with RB1 and TP53 pathway defects.

media.alt_text: Original distal-femur schematic showing sunburst periosteal reaction and Codman triangle beside malignant osteoid histology.

references.citation: USMLE. Step 1 Exam Content: Content Outline and Specifications. Accessed August 4, 2026.
National Cancer Institute. Osteosarcoma and Undifferentiated Pleomorphic Sarcoma of Bone Treatment (PDQ). Accessed August 4, 2026.

taxonomy.subtopic: B-cell infection and reactive CD8-positive atypical lymphocytes

questions.stem_html: A 20-year-old student has fever, exudative pharyngitis, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly. A heterophile-antibody test is positive. The accompanying smear schematic shows large lymphocytes with abundant basophilic cytoplasm molding around erythrocytes. Which cells make up most of these atypical circulating lymphocytes?

options.text_html: EBV-infected memory B cells undergoing lytic replication
Natural killer cells activated by absent MHC class I
Plasma cells secreting heterophile IgM
CD4-positive helper T cells responding to capsid antigen
Activated CD8-positive cytotoxic T cells responding to EBV-infected B cells

questions.explanation_html: EBV infects B lymphocytes by binding CD21. The prominent atypical lymphocytes seen in infectious mononucleosis are not the infected B cells themselves; they are reactive, activated CD8-positive cytotoxic T lymphocytes responding to EBV-infected B cells. Their expansion accounts for much of the lymphocytosis and the characteristic smear appearance.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: EBV-infected B cells are the targets of the response but do not constitute most of the atypical lymphocytes on the smear.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: Natural killer cells participate in antiviral defense but are not the predominant atypical population in classic infectious mononucleosis.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Plasma cells may produce antibodies, but they do not create the characteristic broad-cytoplasm atypical lymphocytosis.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: CD4 T cells contribute to immunity, but the major expanded atypical population is CD8-positive.

questions.educational_objective: EBV uses CD21 to infect B cells, while the atypical lymphocytes of infectious mononucleosis are predominantly reactive CD8-positive T cells.

media.alt_text: Original schematic showing EBV binding CD21 on a B cell and a reactive CD8 T cell with characteristic atypical lymphocyte morphology.

references.citation: USMLE. Step 1 Exam Content: Content Outline and Specifications. Accessed August 4, 2026.
NCBI Bookshelf/IARC. Epstein-Barr Virus and Kaposi's Sarcoma Herpesvirus. Accessed August 4, 2026.

taxonomy.subtopic: HHV-8 spindle-cell vascular proliferation in immunodeficiency

questions.stem_html: A man with untreated HIV infection and a CD4 count of 70/mm3 develops multiple violaceous plaques on the legs and hard palate. The accompanying histology diagram shows spindle cells forming irregular slit-like vascular spaces with extravasated erythrocytes. Infection with which agent is required for development of this neoplasm?

options.text_html: Human herpesvirus 8
Epstein-Barr virus
Human papillomavirus 16
Human T-cell lymphotropic virus 1
Cytomegalovirus

questions.explanation_html: Kaposi sarcoma is an HHV-8-associated vascular neoplasm that occurs in several epidemiologic forms, including AIDS-associated disease. Histology shows spindle-cell proliferation, jagged or slit-like vascular spaces, inflammatory cells, and extravasated erythrocytes. Immunodeficiency permits expansion of HHV-8-infected cells and cytokine-driven angiogenic growth.

wrong_choice_explanations.2: EBV is linked to several B-cell and epithelial neoplasms but is not the required virus in Kaposi sarcoma.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: HPV16 is associated with anogenital and oropharyngeal squamous carcinomas.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: HTLV-1 is associated with adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: CMV causes opportunistic infection but not the characteristic spindle-cell vascular tumor.

questions.educational_objective: Kaposi sarcoma is an HHV-8-associated spindle-cell vascular neoplasm with slit-like spaces and red-cell extravasation, especially in immunodeficiency.

media.alt_text: Original schematic showing a violaceous plaque and spindle-cell histology with slit-like vascular spaces and extravasated erythrocytes.

references.citation: USMLE. Step 1 Exam Content: Content Outline and Specifications. Accessed August 4, 2026.
National Cancer Institute. Kaposi Sarcoma Treatment (PDQ). Accessed August 4, 2026.

taxonomy.subtopic: Articular cartilage loss, subchondral sclerosis, and osteophyte formation

questions.stem_html: A 70-year-old woman has knee pain that worsens after prolonged walking and improves with rest. Morning stiffness lasts 10 minutes. The accompanying weight-bearing radiograph schematic shows asymmetric medial joint-space narrowing, marginal osteophytes, and subchondral sclerosis. Which pathologic process best accounts for these findings?

options.text_html: Immune-complex deposition in synovial vessels
Progressive articular-cartilage degeneration with subchondral bone remodeling
Pannus formation driven by autoantibodies against citrullinated proteins
Monosodium urate deposition with neutrophilic synovitis
Bacterial invasion of cartilage through the bloodstream

questions.explanation_html: Osteoarthritis is characterized by focal degeneration and loss of articular cartilage, followed by subchondral bone sclerosis, cyst formation, and osteophyte growth. Symptoms are mechanical: pain increases with use and morning stiffness is brief. The asymmetric joint-space loss and osteophytes distinguish osteoarthritis from inflammatory polyarthritis.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Immune-complex vasculitis is not the central mechanism of degenerative joint disease.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Autoimmune pannus formation is characteristic of rheumatoid arthritis and is associated with prolonged morning stiffness and erosions.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Urate crystals produce episodic acute inflammatory arthritis rather than chronic asymmetric cartilage loss with osteophytes.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Septic arthritis causes acute destructive inflammation and systemic illness, not this gradual mechanical pattern.

questions.educational_objective: Osteoarthritis results from articular-cartilage degeneration and subchondral remodeling, producing joint-space narrowing, sclerosis, cysts, and osteophytes.

media.alt_text: Original knee radiograph and cartilage cross-section showing asymmetric joint-space loss, osteophytes, and subchondral sclerosis.

references.citation: USMLE. Step 1 Exam Content: Content Outline and Specifications. Accessed August 4, 2026.

taxonomy.subtopic: UVB-induced keratinocyte dysplasia and progression to squamous carcinoma

questions.stem_html: An 81-year-old retired farmer has several rough, adherent, erythematous papules on the bald scalp and dorsal hands. The accompanying histology schematic shows parakeratosis and atypical keratinocytes concentrated in the lower epidermis without penetration of the basement membrane. This lesion most directly increases the risk of which malignancy?

options.text_html: Basal-cell carcinoma
Melanoma
Cutaneous squamous-cell carcinoma
Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans
Merkel-cell carcinoma

questions.explanation_html: The lesion is actinic keratosis, a UV-induced proliferation of dysplastic epidermal keratinocytes on chronically sun-exposed skin. Atypia is often prominent in the basal and lower epidermis, and lesions may progress to squamous-cell carcinoma in situ or invasive cutaneous squamous-cell carcinoma. Absence of dermal invasion distinguishes the premalignant lesion from invasive cancer.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Basal-cell carcinoma is also related to ultraviolet exposure but is not the direct malignant progression of actinic keratosis.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: Melanoma arises from melanocytes rather than dysplastic keratinocytes.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans is a dermal spindle-cell tumor unrelated to actinic keratosis.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Merkel-cell carcinoma is a neuroendocrine skin cancer and is not the expected progression.

questions.educational_objective: Actinic keratosis is UV-induced keratinocyte dysplasia confined to the epidermis and is a precursor of cutaneous squamous-cell carcinoma.

media.alt_text: Original sun-exposed skin and histology schematic showing parakeratosis and lower-epidermal keratinocyte atypia without dermal invasion.

references.citation: USMLE. Step 1 Exam Content: Content Outline and Specifications. Accessed August 4, 2026.
NCBI Bookshelf. Actinic Keratosis. Accessed August 4, 2026.

taxonomy.subtopic: Sarcoptes burrows and delayed hypersensitivity pruritus

questions.stem_html: Several members of a household develop intense nocturnal pruritus. Examination shows thin, serpiginous burrows in the finger webs and flexor wrists. The accompanying epidermal cross-section contains a mite, eggs, and fecal pellets in the stratum corneum. Why may a patient's first infestation remain minimally symptomatic for several weeks before severe itching begins?

options.text_html: The mite must first invade dermal blood vessels and cause immune-complex vasculitis
Mite eggs must hatch into larvae that directly activate nociceptors
Protective IgG must fall below a critical serum concentration
Sensitization is required before a delayed T-cell response to mite antigens and products develops
The parasite must acquire bacterial superinfection before producing pruritus

questions.explanation_html: Scabies symptoms are largely caused by a delayed hypersensitivity response to the mite and its eggs and fecal products. During a first infestation, sensitization takes time, so pruritus may be delayed for weeks. Previously exposed patients can become symptomatic much sooner because memory immune responses are already present. The distribution and nocturnal itching are classic clues.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Scabies mites remain mainly within the stratum corneum and do not need to invade dermal vessels.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: Egg hatching contributes to the life cycle but does not explain the characteristic delayed onset of the first immune-mediated symptoms.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Loss of protective IgG is not the mechanism of delayed initial pruritus.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Bacterial superinfection can complicate scratching but is not required for the primary itching syndrome.

questions.educational_objective: Scabies produces nocturnal pruritus and burrows; symptoms reflect delayed hypersensitivity to mites and their products after sensitization.

media.alt_text: Original hand-distribution map and epidermal cross-section showing a Sarcoptes burrow with mite, eggs, and fecal pellets.

references.citation: USMLE. Step 1 Exam Content: Content Outline and Specifications. Accessed August 4, 2026.
CDC. Clinical Care of Scabies and About Scabies. Accessed August 4, 2026.

taxonomy.subtopic: Resorption distal to airway obstruction and ipsilateral mediastinal shift

questions.stem_html: Two days after abdominal surgery, a patient develops tachypnea and reduced breath sounds over the right upper chest. The accompanying radiograph schematic shows a dense right-upper-lobe opacity, elevation of the right hemidiaphragm, and displacement of the trachea toward the right. Which mechanism best explains the direction of mediastinal displacement?

options.text_html: Air enters the pleural space through a one-way valve and raises intrathoracic pressure
A large pleural effusion pushes the mediastinum away from the affected side
Diffuse bronchospasm causes dynamic hyperinflation of the affected lung
Pulmonary hemorrhage increases the mass of the affected lobe
Gas distal to an obstructing mucus plug is absorbed, producing ipsilateral volume loss

questions.explanation_html: Obstructive, or resorption, atelectasis occurs when an airway is blocked, often by a postoperative mucus plug. Distal gas is absorbed into the blood, the affected lobe loses volume, and adjacent structures are pulled toward the collapse. Elevated hemidiaphragm, fissure displacement, and ipsilateral mediastinal shift distinguish volume loss from tension pneumothorax or a large effusion, which push structures away.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Tension pneumothorax increases ipsilateral pressure and shifts the mediastinum away from the affected side.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: A large effusion exerts mass effect and usually shifts the mediastinum contralaterally.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Bronchospasm causes air trapping rather than focal lobar opacity with volume loss.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Hemorrhage can create opacity but does not characteristically pull the mediastinum toward the lesion.

questions.educational_objective: Airway obstruction causes distal gas resorption and lung-volume loss, pulling the mediastinum toward the atelectatic side.

media.alt_text: Original chest schematic comparing obstructive atelectasis with volume loss and ipsilateral shift against tension pneumothorax with contralateral shift.

references.citation: USMLE. Step 1 Exam Content: Content Outline and Specifications. Accessed August 4, 2026.
NCBI Bookshelf. Atelectasis. Accessed August 4, 2026.

taxonomy.subtopic: TGF-beta-driven collagen deposition beyond original wound boundaries

questions.stem_html: A 24-year-old woman develops a firm, smooth, pruritic scar after an ear piercing. Over the next year, the scar continues to enlarge beyond the original puncture margins. The accompanying comparison diagram shows this lesion extending into previously uninjured skin. Which process best explains the lesion?

options.text_html: Persistent fibroblast activation with excessive collagen deposition beyond the original wound, promoted by TGF-beta signaling
Failure of neutrophils to remove bacteria during the inflammatory phase
Deficient type III collagen synthesis during the proliferative phase
Excessive collagen degradation by matrix metalloproteinases
Autoantibody-mediated destruction of dermal elastic fibers

questions.explanation_html: A keloid is an abnormal scar that extends beyond the boundaries of the original injury and may continue to grow. It reflects persistent fibroblast activity and excessive extracellular-matrix, particularly collagen, deposition, with profibrotic signaling that includes TGF-beta. A hypertrophic scar is raised but remains confined to the original wound.

wrong_choice_explanations.2: Infection can delay healing but does not produce the characteristic progressive extension beyond wound borders.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Deficient collagen synthesis causes fragile or poorly healed wounds rather than a bulky expanding scar.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Excessive matrix degradation would reduce, not increase, scar mass.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Autoimmune elastic-fiber destruction is not the mechanism of a keloid.

questions.educational_objective: Keloids are TGF-beta-associated fibroproliferative scars that extend beyond the original wound; hypertrophic scars remain confined to it.

media.alt_text: Original side-by-side diagram showing a hypertrophic scar confined to the wound and a keloid extending beyond the original wound boundaries.

references.citation: USMLE. Step 1 Exam Content: Content Outline and Specifications. Accessed August 4, 2026.
NCBI Bookshelf. Hypertrophic Scarring and Keloids. Accessed August 4, 2026.

taxonomy.subtopic: C5-C6 injury and Erb-Duchenne posture

questions.stem_html: After a difficult delivery complicated by shoulder dystocia, a newborn holds the affected arm adducted and internally rotated with the elbow extended and the forearm pronated. The accompanying brachial-plexus diagram highlights one proximal segment. Injury to which structure best explains the loss of shoulder abduction, external rotation, elbow flexion, and forearm supination?

options.text_html: Lower trunk formed by C8-T1
Upper trunk formed by C5-C6
Posterior cord containing C5-T1 fibers
Medial cord containing C8-T1 fibers
Long thoracic nerve formed by C5-C7

questions.explanation_html: The posture is Erb-Duchenne palsy from traction injury to the upper trunk of the brachial plexus, formed mainly by C5-C6. Weakness affects deltoid and supraspinatus-mediated abduction, infraspinatus-mediated external rotation, biceps and brachialis-mediated elbow flexion, and biceps-mediated supination, producing the classic waiter's-tip posture.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Lower-trunk injury causes hand weakness and sensory loss along the medial forearm and hand, not the described proximal posture.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: A posterior-cord lesion would affect radial and axillary distributions more broadly and would not selectively reproduce the classic C5-C6 pattern.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: A medial-cord lesion mainly affects ulnar and medial median-nerve functions.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Long thoracic nerve injury causes scapular winging due to serratus anterior weakness, not elbow-flexion and supination loss.

questions.educational_objective: Erb-Duchenne palsy localizes to the C5-C6 upper trunk and causes loss of shoulder abduction/external rotation and elbow flexion/supination.

taxonomy.subtopic: Unopposed neutrophil elastase and misfolded hepatic protein retention

questions.stem_html: A 38-year-old nonsmoker has progressive dyspnea, lower-lobe-predominant panacinar emphysema, and mildly elevated aminotransferases. Liver biopsy contains periodic acid-Schiff-positive, diastase-resistant cytoplasmic globules. Which paired mechanism best explains the pulmonary and hepatic findings?

options.text_html: Defective chloride transport in airway epithelium; copper accumulation in hepatocytes
Autoantibodies against alveolar basement membrane; iron accumulation in hepatocytes
Unopposed neutrophil elastase in the lung; retention of misfolded protein in hepatocytes
Failure of surfactant recycling; lysosomal glycogen accumulation in hepatocytes
Reduced ciliary motility; alpha-galactosidase deficiency in hepatocytes

questions.explanation_html: Alpha-1 antitrypsin normally inhibits neutrophil elastase in the lung. Deficiency permits elastase-mediated destruction of alveolar walls, producing panacinar emphysema that is often lower-lobe predominant. In common severe deficiency alleles, abnormal alpha-1 antitrypsin misfolds and accumulates within hepatocyte endoplasmic reticulum, creating PAS-positive, diastase-resistant globules and causing liver injury.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Defective chloride transport describes cystic fibrosis, and hepatic copper accumulation describes Wilson disease.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: Anti-basement-membrane antibodies cause pulmonary-renal disease; iron overload causes hemochromatosis.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Surfactant-recycling disorders and glycogen storage do not create the characteristic lung-liver pairing.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Ciliary dyskinesia causes recurrent sinopulmonary disease, and alpha-galactosidase deficiency causes Fabry disease.

questions.educational_objective: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency causes emphysema through unopposed elastase and liver disease through intracellular retention of misfolded protein.

taxonomy.subtopic: Terminal ileal bile-salt loss, fat malabsorption, and calcium oxalate stones

questions.stem_html: A patient with Crohn disease undergoes resection of the terminal ileum. Months later, the patient develops recurrent radiopaque kidney stones composed of calcium oxalate. The accompanying intestinal diagram shows unabsorbed fatty acids, luminal calcium, and oxalate entering the colon. Which change most directly increases urinary oxalate?

options.text_html: Increased hepatic conversion of glycine to oxalate after bile-salt depletion
Reduced renal calcium reabsorption caused by secondary hyperparathyroidism
Direct secretion of oxalate by inflamed ileal mucosa
Binding of luminal calcium by fatty acids, leaving free oxalate available for colonic absorption
Reduced citrate absorption causing isolated hypocitraturia without altered oxalate handling

questions.explanation_html: Terminal-ileal disease or resection causes bile-salt malabsorption and fat malabsorption. Unabsorbed fatty acids bind luminal calcium, so less calcium is available to precipitate oxalate in the intestine. Free oxalate is then absorbed in the colon, producing enteric hyperoxaluria and calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Endogenous hepatic oxalate production is not the primary mechanism after ileal disease.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: Secondary hyperparathyroidism can alter calcium balance but does not explain the characteristic increase in intestinal oxalate absorption.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Inflamed ileum does not secrete enough oxalate to account for enteric hyperoxaluria.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Hypocitraturia can increase stone risk, but the mechanism illustrated specifically increases free oxalate absorption.

questions.educational_objective: Terminal-ileal bile-salt loss causes fat malabsorption; fatty acids bind calcium, freeing oxalate for colonic absorption and causing enteric hyperoxaluria.

taxonomy.subtopic: Optic-chiasm compression and bitemporal hemianopia

questions.stem_html: A 44-year-old woman has progressive headaches and difficulty seeing cars approaching from either side. Formal testing shows loss of the temporal visual fields in both eyes. The accompanying sellar diagram shows a mass expanding superiorly from the pituitary fossa. Which fibers are compressed?

options.text_html: Uncrossed temporal retinal fibers in both optic nerves
Optic tracts carrying ipsilateral temporal fields
Meyer loops carrying superior visual-field information
Occipital cortex representing the macula
Crossing nasal retinal fibers at the optic chiasm

questions.explanation_html: Nasal retinal fibers receive light from the temporal visual fields and cross in the optic chiasm. A pituitary macroadenoma expanding superiorly compresses the central chiasm, damaging these crossing fibers and causing bitemporal hemianopia. More posterior lesions of the optic tract or radiations produce homonymous defects rather than temporal loss in both eyes.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Temporal retinal fibers remain uncrossed and carry nasal visual-field information.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: Each optic tract carries the contralateral visual hemifield from both eyes, so tract lesions cause homonymous hemianopia.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Meyer-loop lesions cause contralateral superior quadrantanopia.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Occipital lesions produce contralateral homonymous field defects, often with macular sparing.

questions.educational_objective: Pituitary macroadenomas compress crossing nasal retinal fibers in the optic chiasm, producing bitemporal hemianopia.

taxonomy.subtopic: Premature trypsin activation, fat necrosis, and hypocalcemia

questions.stem_html: A man with heavy alcohol use develops severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, vomiting, and elevated serum lipase. Imaging shows pancreatic edema and extensive peripancreatic fat stranding. Two days later, serum calcium falls. The accompanying diagram shows chalky deposits in necrotic fat. Which process most directly explains the hypocalcemia?

options.text_html: Released fatty acids bind calcium and form insoluble soaps in areas of fat necrosis
Calcitonin secretion increases because pancreatic enzymes activate thyroid C cells
Renal calcium excretion rises due to acute inhibition of proximal sodium reabsorption
Damaged acinar cells secrete excess glucagon, shifting calcium into bone
Trypsin directly cleaves circulating parathyroid hormone

questions.explanation_html: Premature intrapancreatic activation of trypsin initiates autodigestion and activates other enzymes, including lipase. Lipase-mediated fat necrosis releases free fatty acids that bind calcium, forming insoluble calcium soaps, a process called saponification. Extensive fat necrosis can therefore lower serum calcium and appears grossly as chalky deposits.

wrong_choice_explanations.2: Calcitonin excess is not a recognized consequence of pancreatic enzyme activation.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Renal calcium wasting is not the principal mechanism of pancreatitis-associated hypocalcemia.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Glucagon does not drive acute calcium deposition into bone in this setting.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Trypsin-mediated parathyroid hormone cleavage is not the established explanation.

questions.educational_objective: Acute pancreatitis causes enzyme-mediated fat necrosis; released fatty acids bind calcium to form soaps, producing hypocalcemia.
